#35844. Jensen Huang’s Return Demonstrates Nvidia Is Too Big to Police

Jensen Huang’s Return Demonstrates Nvidia Is Too Big to Police

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too vital to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED.
  • In a recent development, nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security.
  • Industry observers note that president Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too vital to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.

In a recent development, nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore tech giant Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.

The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.

Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.

“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” claims Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”.

Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The Fresh York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.

“Some tech companies have become so big—and so notable to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” notes Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics.

Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he indicates. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says.

According to recent reports, emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, states the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says.

On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease notes it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the newly introduced controls,” she says.

Industry observers note that the board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he said.).

Nvidia did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

According to recent reports, whether Huang broke any laws is a separate question from whether Beijing gained anything through him. “Did [the assurances] reflect a counterintelligence damage assessment by the intelligence community or the FBI, or were they political in nature?” says Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously directed the Foreign Malign Influence Center at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. “Lawmakers should press on that.”.

Senior officials may have seen intelligence that isn’t public, so the assurances shouldn’t just be dismissed, says Sunny Cheung, a China studies fellow at the Jamestown Foundation. “However, we still don’t know who provided those assurances, what evidence they reviewed, or how they reached their conclusion, particularly when Nvidia’s own independent investigation remains unfinished,” he says.

Sources indicate that lawmakers appear to have seen little of that evidence. At a briefing this month by CIA director John Ratcliffe and Clayton that was scheduled to cover Iran, lawmakers pressed for answers about Huang, and the responses left some of them puzzled, according to the Times. A follow-up briefing for senior national security staff was postponed.

Cheung says the Ministry of State Security may not have needed Nvidia’s secrets to profit from the relationship. “From a counterintelligence perspective, I think people are too focused on whether Jensen handed over trade secrets,” he says. “China’s Ministry of State Security wouldn’t necessarily need Nvidia’s next-generation chip blueprints to benefit from access to him.” Insight into Huang’s direct conversations with the president, senior officials, and other top tech executives, along with his views on China and Taiwan and his role in Washington’s export-control debate, “could already be extremely valuable to Beijing,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that brandt sees the same mix of risks. “Information about Nvidia’s proprietary chip designs could help China advance its own chip design efforts,” she indicates. “Insight into Nvidia’s conversations with the White House and Congress could help Beijing anticipate where US export control policy is headed.” Investigators should also ask whether Alice Huang compromised Huang’s devices, what security clearance he held, and whether he still holds it, she says.

Recent findings suggest that huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to roll back restrictions on Nvidia’s chip sales to China and negotiated a deal giving the US government a 25 percent cut of sales of certain chips approved for export there, the Times has reported. In April, minister of state security Chen Yixin made overcoming the “blockades” that limit China’s access to key technologies like AI a sixth core mission for his ministry, known as the MSS. Alice Huang’s network of chip-buying companies “lines up precisely” with that mission, Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Trump’s first term, told the paper.

“A further question is whether Alice Huang was tasked by Chinese intelligence to influence Jensen Huang's views or approach to US export restrictions on China, and, if so, to what extent she succeeded,” Peterson says. The Journal also reported that the intelligence is inconclusive on whether she was actively tasked to collect information on Huang, and Cheung says “whether any such information was obtained or influence exercised remains unproven.”.

Megaspeed’s purchases are better documented. A Malaysian subsidiary bought at least $4.8 billion worth of equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records the Times reviewed. Its subsidiaries have also served Chinese clients, including Alibaba. US intelligence indicates that Alice Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from spring 2025 until this fall, and that her business partner, Kang Wei, also worked with the agency, the paper reported Sunday. Her network has been linked to efforts to supply Nvidia chips to China’s state-owned military contractors. Enough has been reported to suggest that Huang, “wittingly or not, may have played a role in helping Megaspeed as it sought access to advanced Nvidia chips,” Kilcrease claims.

Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nicholas Eftimiades, a former CIA and Defense Intelligence Agency officer who teaches homeland security at Penn State Harrisburg, notes Huang himself poses no security risk. Now that the relationship is public, he says, Huang has little chance of unwittingly passing along more information about US government policy or Nvidia’s board deliberations. Peterson agrees that scrutiny from Nvidia’s board, its compliance staff, federal agencies, and Congress likely limits any further exposure. But “we are still in the dark as to whether any sensitive information may already have been compromised,” she says, “or whether any resulting harm can be identified or mitigated.”.

According to recent reports, huang’s defenders have repeatedly noted that he never received a defensive briefing, a warning the government sometimes gives Americans whom foreign intelligence services target. Nvidia’s board notes its investigation will continue with Huang’s cooperation, and the company is searching for a chief compliance officer. A committee of independent directors is examining whether Huang shared corporate or national security information with Alice Huang. The board has also formed a new committee of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.

Peterson states the manufacturer’s leadership matters. “Nvidia is an exceptionally important company, and there are legitimate arguments about the implications of losing its leadership at a critical moment in the global AI race,” she says. “But those considerations should not determine the conclusions of national security investigations.”.

Sources indicate that trump told CNBC Monday that keeping the United States ahead of China made reinstating Huang imperative. “If we didn't do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’” he mentioned.

For Brandt, the bigger cost may come with Washington’s next warning. “This erodes the credibility of US government warnings about China’s technological ambitions and how far it will go to achieve them,” she indicates. “How will those warnings land going forward, both with our own companies and with foreign governments? We risk making a hard problem harder: emboldening Beijing while weakening our own defenses.”.

That cost extends to the allies Washington depends on to police its controls, adds Sarah Bauerle Danzman, an associate professor of international studies at Indiana University’s Hamilton Lugar School. The Commerce Department has few enforcement agents abroad to monitor transshipment, she says, so the system relies on partner countries to run checks and share information about problematic buyers. Singapore says it repeatedly raised concerns with US authorities in this case.

“These types of incidents make such cooperation more difficult to sustain,” Bauerle Danzman states.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on December 1 and 2. “The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now [borne] by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens,” Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, remarked on X.

“I think Congress has gotten fed up,” says Kilcrease, who cites bipartisan concern about Megaspeed and what she calls the administration’s broader accommodation of China. “We can expect hearings and investigations from multiple committees, and Congress is highly motivated to pass legislation to tighten export controls, increase its oversight of administration decisions, and bolster enforcement.”.

Industry observers note that “Jensen may be back, and he should not be presumed guilty of wrongdoing,” Cheung says. “But his reinstatement should not be mistaken for a clean bill of health. Nvidia and the administration still have important questions to answer.”.

Latest Update: Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.
  • The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people.
  • Sources indicate that local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.

The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate.

Sources indicate that local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast.

Lead is a neurotoxin that does not break down in the environment and poses significant health risks, particularly to young children and pregnant people.

Sources indicate that in the hours leading to the detonation, the Army released maps showing modeled drift and distribution of the plume. They indicated that airborne lead would travel around 100 miles to the southwest of the facility, while dust deposition would cover around 200 square miles in that direction. Researchers and government workers have already collected air and soil samples from the area, which will act as baseline readings for lead levels in the aftermath and fallout of the detonation.

In preparation for the blast, the Army surrounded the earth-covered containers with sand-and lime fill. They set up water cannons and misters intended to keep dust down. They also covered the top of the container with fire-suppressant foam. The Army documented the efforts with a video posted to social media Wednesday morning.

The explosion follows days of confusion, outrage, questions, and delays. Although the Army remarked that it has known about the hazardous state of the lead azide since March, Iowans were largely unaware of the situation and the planned detonation until last week. At that time, the Army had planned to detonate the barrels on Friday, November 20. But public alarm and an emergency court filing from environmental groups led to a delay, which was initially scheduled for Monday, then Tuesday, and finally to today.

A federal appeals court initially issued a stay on the Army’s permit to conduct the detonation, and, on Monday, Trump said he ordered the military to halt the operation until the court lifted the stay and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat, signed off. Ultimately, the court ruled this week that the Army could move ahead with prepares, given no better option.

But questions continue to swirl about how the lead azide got to such a “catastrophically hazardous condition.” On Tuesday, The Washington Post reported that it had viewed emails that suggest the Army knew since at least September 2025, not this past March.

Latest Update: AWS IoT Core now uses dedicated IPv6 address ranges for the HTTP rule action

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (285 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AWS IoT Core can now send traffic to HTTPS endpoints within a dedicated, published IPv6 address range.
  • It has been revealed that AWS IoT Core is a fully managed service that securely connects IoT devices at scale to the AWS cloud and routes IoT device data to AWS and third-party services.
  • To get started, configure your HTTPS endpoint destination to be reachable only over IPv6 by publishing AAAA DNS records (and removing the A DNS records).

In a recent development, AWS IoT Core can now send traffic to HTTPS endpoints within a dedicated, published IPv6 address range. This launch enables you to configure your HTTPS endpoints to accept requests only from AWS IoT Core and block all other traffic, thereby reducing your endpoint's exposure to public internet.

It has been revealed that AWS IoT Core is a fully managed service that securely connects IoT devices at scale to the AWS cloud and routes IoT device data to AWS and third-party services. AWS IoT Core's HTTP rule action delivers IoT device data to any HTTPS endpoint, such as your application servers, on-premises systems, or partner services. With this launch, you can choose from AWS IoT Core's published IPv6 range, and add the fixed IPv6 range to an Amazon API Gateway resource policy, a security group, or your firewall rules. Your HTTPS endpoints will then accept traffic only from AWS IoT Core, giving you network layer control over who can reach your endpoint.

To get started, configure your HTTPS endpoint destination to be reachable only over IPv6 by publishing AAAA DNS records (and removing the A DNS records). This allows IoT Core's HTTP rule action to use only IPv6 addresses when sending data to your HTTP destination. Then allow AWS IoT Core's published IPv6 range for your Region, and create or enhancement your HTTP rule action with the endpoint destination. Dedicated IPv6 ranges are available at no additional charge in all AWS Global Regions where AWS IoT Core is available, including AWS GovCloud (US). To find the range for your Region, see Restricting HTTP action traffic to the rules engine IPv6 ranges in the AWS IoT Core Developer Guide.

Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.

Why Netflixâs $82B Acquisition Makes Sense in the Era of AI.

Netflix recently entered into a definitive agreement to buy Warner Brothers for over $82B in Enterprise Value. Itâs being called the biggest, most consequential deal in Hollywood history. The purchase comes with intellectual property including Batman, Superman, Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Big Bang Theory, The Sopranos, The Matrix, Lord of the Rings (film rights), Godzilla/MonsterVerse, Mad Max, and Mortal Kombat.

IP like this became more valuable in the internet age, and will become even more valuable in the age of AI. Earlier this year, I published an internal Sequoia memo detailing the implications of AI on the IP industry. Given the substantial news, I thought it would be nice to share a few excerpts with my friends and colleagues more broadly.

On a recent work trip to Paris, a profound irony struck me at the MusÃ©e dâOrsay. The museum, a glorious former train station, is a temple to the Industrial Revolution. Its collection, spanning 1848 to 1914, chronicles the period of historyâs most rapid industrialization.

Edgar Degas: Course de Gentleman (Gentlemenâs Race).

Sources indicate that the art is filled with tributes to this upcoming age: Monet paints locomotives at La Gare Saint-Lazare, smokestacks fill the background of Degasâ Course de Gentlemen, and the Traders in factory-made clothing. It is a museum drenched in the dawn of industrialization.

Claude Monet: La Gare Saint-Lazare.

According to recent reports, this is where the paradox lies. This was the exact moment in history when the cost to reproduce a piece of art dropped precipitously. What was once near-impossible, replicating a masterpiece, became trivially cheap. Logically, as near-perfect copies became ubiquitous, the value of the âoriginalâ should have plummeted. And yet, the opposite happened. The great lesson of the dâOrsay is this: instead of becoming worthless in the age of manufacturing, these original works became priceless. As reproduction became easy, the value and allure of the original only went up.

Edgar Degas: At the Stock Exchange.

Hereâs why IP is well positioned in an AI future:.

If we have AGI, or even inexpensive content creation, that will drive down the cost of intelligence.

That affordable intelligence will be used to create an abundance of content.

Humans will react to abundance with a desire for familiarity and quality.

The value of the âoriginalâ will only increase.

In this era, âoriginalâ works will increase in value quickly.

These âoriginalsâ include art, real estate, and intellectual property.

Intellectual property that has already earned a spot in our minds will benefit disproportionately.

In the AI Era, nostalgic content will benefit disproportionately as it is manifest in countless different ways.

Industry observers note that as content production costs approach zero, the marginal cost of new content will also become negligible, leading to an explosion in content volume. This content flood will profoundly shift the value of attention, the primary currency in this new landscape. Undifferentiated content will rapidly lose value, and consumers will be far less willing to invest time in new content unless itâs algorithmically recommended by dominant platforms. Very few new content concepts will break out, following an extreme Power Law.

According to recent reports, success in this environment will hinge on âattention distribution,â defined as a consumerâs inherent interest in a specific piece of content. Nostalgic content is poised to become the most valuable. In a world saturated with novelty, authentic nostalgic content will be incredibly difficult to simulate accurately; even slight deviations from the original will feel inauthentic and cheap.

Consumers will be willing to pay for nostalgic content due to its relatively low cost. For parents, the decision to purchase authentic nostalgic content for their children over a knockoff, especially when the real item is priced reasonably, becomes a clear choice.

The Impending Content Deluge and the Scarcity of Attention.

The ubiquity of General AI will drastically reduce the marginal cost of content production, approaching zero. This will unleash an unprecedented explosion in content volume, creating a hyper-saturated information environment. In this landscape, human attention, rather than content itself, will become the primary scarce resource and the dominant currency. Undifferentiated content, easily replicable and ubiquitous, will rapidly depreciate in value. Consumers, overwhelmed by choice, will increasingly rely on algorithmic recommendations from dominant content platforms to filter and curate their experiences, leading to a profound shift in content discovery and consumption patterns.

Attention Distribution: The Upcoming Competitive Moat.

Recent findings suggest that success in this AI-driven content economy will hinge on âattention distribution,â defined as a consumerâs inherent and deeply ingrained interest in a specific piece of content. This is distinct from mere algorithmic visibility, as it speaks to an intrinsic desire to engage with content. While AI can generate novel content at scale, it will struggle to replicate the nuanced emotional resonance and deeply embedded cultural references that drive genuine attention.

The Inherent Value of Authentic Nostalgic Content.

Nostalgic content is uniquely positioned to become the most valuable asset in this future. The core arguments for its enduring value are:.

Difficulty of Authentic Simulation: While AGI can mimic styles and tropes, accurately simulating authentic nostalgic content will be incredibly challenging. The most popular feature in Sora 2 is their âCameoâ feature, which pulls in authentic characters and people into the AI generated worlds. Even minute deviations from the original, like a slight alteration in a beloved characterâs voice, a subtle anachronism in a period piece, or a deviation in the execution of a well-known narrative, will register as âinauthenticâ or âcheapâ to a discerning audience. The emotional connection to nostalgic content is often rooted in precise, well-remembered details, making it highly resistant to imperfect algorithmic replication. This is akin to the âuncanny valleyâ in robotics, where near-human but imperfect simulations evoke discomfort rather than acceptance.

Consumer Willingness to Pay: Despite the approaching zero marginal cost of content, consumers will demonstrate a significant willingness to pay for authentic nostalgic content.

It has been revealed that as AI democratizes content creation, the landscape will shift dramatically. The true scarcity will be human attention, and the ultimate value will reside in content that can capture and hold that attention through genuine emotional resonance. Authentic nostalgic content, by virtue of its irreplicable emotional depth and its proven ability to connect across generations, represents a highly defensible and appreciating asset in this evolving digital economy. Investors should prioritize companies that control and strategically leverage these invaluable cultural touchstones.

Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.
  • According to recent reports, although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China.
  • The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.

According to recent reports, although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China. In a press release, however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.

The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

According to recent reports, among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its users’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”.

Sources indicate that as the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of Fresh York Joseph Nocella Jr. mentioned that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage tech giant called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

Industry observers note that one of the stolen ideas was the design of a T-Mobile robot called “Tappy,” which helped the US firm “assess the responsiveness of touch screens by mimicking a human touch,” the DOJ said. To copy the design, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement, then sent photos and technical details back to China. Even bolder, when that intel was deemed insufficient, “a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DOJ said.

Huawei’s tactics weren’t always sophisticated, but they were effective, the DOJ mentioned, building into “a long-running conspiracy to steal intellectual property of US companies.” At trade demonstrates and tours of rivals’ facilities, Huawei employees would pretend to “get lost,” the DOJ said, so they could wander into restricted areas and take photos of hardware, The Latest York Times reported.

According to recent reports, huawei engineers would also sometimes hide their activity by spelling words backwards. For example, Huawei was able to copy the source code used on Cisco routers—which the DOJ stated was “identified as the ‘crown jewel’ of Cisco technology”—by taking notes in which they spelled Cisco as “ocsic.” Another time, the DOJ noted that a Huawei employee was caught “photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment” while wearing a badge that falsely identified him as an employee of “Weihua.”.

During the trial, Meredith Arfa, a federal prosecutor, noted that Huawei employees were sometimes paid bonuses for their crimes, since the theft was so integral to Huawei’s business model, NYT reported.

Roman Rozhavsky, the assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said that Huawei spent years expanding its international enterprise “through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of US companies and the rule of law.”.

Huawei has been banned from selling its tech in the US since 2019, so NYT noted that the guilty verdict is unlikely to rattle the firm’s finances much. However, the financial penalties stemming from the verdict could be steep, as the DOJ explained that they include “criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution.”.

Sentencing is scheduled for September 14.

Recent findings suggest that huawei continues to deny any wrongdoing and rejects US claims that the Chinese Communist Party directed the thefts. NYT noted that Huawei’s investors have argued that the US fight is politically motivated and seeks to hobble “a Chinese initiative to build 5G networks around the world.”.

In a recent development, outside the courthouse following the verdict, Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that it’s significant that the jury did not convict Huawei of racketeering charges or conspiracy to obstruct justice. According to Heberlig, the examples of US technology theft merely represented “isolated misconduct by manufacturer employees,” which inevitably happens in a company so large, with “hundreds of thousands of people.”.

Heberlig confirmed that Huawei planned to appeal and considered the jury’s opposition to racketeering charges to be a “profound rejection of the United States’ narratives about what Huawei is.”.

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hard-working company that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” Heberlig stated.

After the verdict, China “lashed out” at the US, AFP reported. According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, the US is trying to use the ruling to “suppress” Huawei.

China “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” Guo noted.

However, the FBI’s Rozhavsky suggested that even China, which frequently negotiates with Trump as the trade rivals continually clash, can’t spare Huawei from substantial penalties.

“This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation,” Rozhavsky noted. “No manufacturer is too significant, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the US and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Transcribe Turbo, our next-generation speech-to-text model, is now in public preview in US East (Ohio) for batch and streaming. Turbo improves accuracy, supports custom vocabulary, and formats numbers, dates, currency, phone numbers and addresses following each locale's conventions.

Streaming: English, Portuguese, French, Italian, German and Spanish supported. Word Error Rate (WER) drops ~14% relative in English and 11% relative in the other languages versus the current production model, and formatting accuracy improves by more than 20 points.

Sources indicate that batch: English Turbo is generally available in most AWS Regions. Portuguese, French, Italian, German, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Arabic are now in preview, with ~16% lower word error rate.

The base model needs no API, code, or SDK changes.

Turbo streaming also adds two fresh features for voice agents in English at launch and for other languages by the end of December 2026.

Recent findings suggest that semantic turn-taking detects when a caller is done speaking from what they said and their prosody in speech, not silence alone. It won't cut callers off mid-sentence ("I'd like to transfer… $250 to savings") or make short answers like "yes", "no" wait on silence timeouts. It responds in about 615 ms with a 5% interruption rate, and you can tune it.

In a recent development, runtime ASR hints give your agent context at every turn. Unlike static custom vocabulary, set once per session, hints enable your client application to send menu options, expected names and the expected entity type (date, phone number, currency) before each turn. On English customer service data, hints raise menu-routing accuracy from 87% to 97%.

It has been revealed that both features come at no additional charge. To try them, turn on EndOfTurnDetection and send hints in a ConfigureEvent.

Learn more in the Builder Center blog and the sample voice agent on GitHub.

“Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”.

Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the company had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”.

He mentioned he still prepares on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

Sources indicate that “I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he said. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”.

He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

“This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he said.

The fracas began earlier this month, when the company first proposed latest contractual language. The updated terms read:.

As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”.

Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account people to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

Industry observers note that “Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the company’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today, AWS introduces the general availability of ELB for Envoy, a fresh load balancer type in Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) that runs open-source Envoy proxies.
  • You can bring your existing Envoy configurations, extensions, and control planes as they are, and add AWS integrations such as AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and AWS WAF with minimal configuration.
  • Industry observers note that you can add custom logic with WebAssembly, Lua scripting, or external processing.

Recent findings suggest that today, AWS introduces the general availability of ELB for Envoy, a fresh load balancer type in Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) that runs open-source Envoy proxies. Platform teams that run Envoy themselves own upgrades, security patching, and capacity across Availability Zones (AZs). ELB for Envoy takes on that work. Each load balancer runs its proxies on dedicated Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances with hardware isolation from the AWS Nitro System, so a zero-day in Envoy stays contained to your load balancer. ELB for Envoy also monitors for security vulnerabilities (CVEs) and applies Envoy and operating system patches automatically, so you can focus on your applications instead of your proxy fleet.

You can bring your existing Envoy configurations, extensions, and control planes as they are, and add AWS integrations such as AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and AWS WAF with minimal configuration. If you run Envoy Gateway on Kubernetes, install the ELB for Envoy remote infrastructure provider alongside Envoy Gateway to move your proxies to ELB for Envoy without rewriting your Gateway API resources.

Industry observers note that you can add custom logic with WebAssembly, Lua scripting, or external processing. ELB for Envoy runs inside your VPC, integrates with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) security groups, and supports VPC encryption. It's well suited to workloads that need Envoy's extensibility, such as custom authentication, request transformation, or advanced traffic routing, along with Kubernetes ingress and migrations from self-managed Envoy.

At general availability, ELB for Envoy is available in 14 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Stockholm), Europe (Spain), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), and Asia Pacific (Thailand). To learn more, visit the ELB for Envoy product page, ELB pricing page, and documentation. To get started, visit the AWS Management Console.

Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements.
  • Sources indicate that after four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux.
  • Ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault.

Sources indicate that after four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.

Ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”.

Nearly the entire modern web right now runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.

An independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every latest browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.

In a recent development, the Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a upcoming independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.

The Ladybird alpha is a rolling release channel that updates automatically, and the downloadable package is a huge step to getting the browser onto the PCs of everyday users. “Ladybird improves swiftly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that,” Kling wrote. Though the browser began as C++, in keeping with the ethos of SerenityOS, the project has since started shifting toward Rust, starting with its JavaScript engine.

While it’s exciting to have a new engine option for browsing, the project leader notes that this is still a very early release. The browser build contains a built-in tool for reporting any websites that fail to render or crash the browser. Kling writes, “We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today.”.

Microsoft owners are still out in the cold on this one for now. The project says that future support for Windows is planned, but it’s macOS and Linux only for now.

I tested the Ladybird alpha version 2026.47.8 on my AceMagic W1 mini PC AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS with 16GB DDR5 and running Fedora Linux 44 with the upcoming KDE Plasma 6.8.3, and the most surprising thing about the alpha build was how little it feels like alpha software.

The browser seemed to handle most anything I threw at it without concern. Day-to-day tabbed browsing mechanics felt snappy and normal. A 50MB test video file downloaded quickly and smoothly. With a dozen tabs open, switching between them was instant, and the browser felt responsive throughout. Options menus were surprisingly fleshed out for a build this young.

Google Maps loaded instantly, located me, and handled everything I threw at it: adding and removing layers, zooming out from the Midwest, and dropping into Street View in Alberta, Canada in around three seconds. Everything rendered fast enough that my mini PC’s fan spun up noticeably. GitHub’s site, including repository navigation, worked without a hitch. So did YouTube and the news sites I tried.

I could stall the browser, but it took some effort. With about 10 tabs open, I was streaming a 4K test video file from my personal Jellyfin server. Everything worked fine at first, but after skipping around in the file over and over again, the browser eventually got stuck. Mind you, this is an alpha build that I was trying to trip up, not a representation of something inherently broken.

According to recent reports, after spending an evening with Ladybird, I can say that while it won’t be replacing Firefox for me anytime soon, I was genuinely impressed that a scratch-made engine could perform this well in such an early state. Most fresh browser projects are forks of something that already exists. Ladybird is the rare exception, an engine written from nothing, and the alpha runs well enough that if you have a Mac or Linux PC handy, it’s worth downloading a build and poking around yourself. Just remember Kling’s warning: This is nowhere near trustworthy enough to make your daily driver, yet.

It has been revealed that what the alpha demonstrates is that a small team of independent developers, funded by donations, has built a browser engine from scratch that handles real web browsing without a fuss. That it works this well this soon, using no existing engine code, is an achievement. I thought I was a Firefox loyalist, but I’ll be keeping an eye on where this one goes.

Jake, Alex and their team are giving IT teams the power to bring AI automation from their own department to every part of the organization.

Jake, Alex and their team are giving IT teams the power to bring AI automation from their own department to every part of the organization.

IT is one of the most critical functions inside any manufacturer. Every employee depends on it, every system flows through it, and almost every operational challenge eventually becomes an IT problem. When IT slows down, everyone feels it: employees are blocked waiting on support, onboarding is painful, rolling out new tools gets bottlenecked, and entire company initiatives end up stalled.

Yet despite ITâs central role, the last decade of tooling has not truly empowered them. The powerful tools are heavy to set up and brittle to maintain; the easy-to-use tools focus on narrow use cases and deflection rather than true automation. IT teams are eager to automate and are more technical than business people. They have experimented with scripts, workflow builders, and more, but the limitations of all these tools still force them to spend the majority of their time on manual work, preventing them from focusing on higher-impact work and enabling the rest of their organizations.

Industry observers note that jake and Alex, the co-founders of Serval, experienced this firsthand at Verkada, where they led Product and Engineering and sold primarily to IT teams. They heard the same half-joking request countless times, and it wasnât about Verkadaâs products. They would ask customers, âWhat else can we build for you?â and IT leaders would reply, âCan you fix my helpdesk too?â These conversations led them to two key insights:.

The first was that true automation only works if it is faster to automate something forever than to do it manually once.

It has been revealed that the second came from watching the few IT leaders who did take the time to build automations. They would first describe the workflow in one simple sentence, then reveal a sprawling tree of branches, nodes, conditions, and edge cases. Jake and Alex wondered: what if you could actually build the entire automation the same way you describe it? What if one simple sentence truly was enough?

These insights were not possible to execute on in the past. Prior generations of AI were not strong enough to make it work, which meant IT teams continued working through manual tasks. That has now changed. With modern LLMs, code generation, and reasoning capabilities, it is finally possible to build a platform where âautomate foreverâ is faster than âfix once.â.

Sources indicate that serval is built precisely to deliver on this, and the team is not stopping there. They are using this moment not only to build a system of automation, but to rethink the entire ITSM system of record. As our own Sequoia IT leader, Leon, shared when they chose to become a Serval customer: âServal is not AI for ITSM â it is ITSM built from AI.â.

Recent findings suggest that at the heart of the platform is an AI automation engine that lets teams go from a simple sentence to a deployment-ready automation. IT can describe workflows in natural language, then refine them further â either in natural language or all the way down to code when needed. This combination of being simple enough for anyone to use, yet deep enough for the most advanced IT builders, has resonated strongly with customers. The workflows are fully explainable and traceable, with all necessary permissions included, giving IT teams complete visibility and control and eliminating hallucination risk.

It has been revealed that while their automation engine integrates with existing systems of records, Serval has also built a full-fledged ITSM platform, including a ticketing system, an access management product, an asset management solution, and more. Serval is both the system of engagement and the system of record. This gives IT a single place to build and orchestrate automations, enforce security and compliance, and capture the data that compounds their automation over time.

Customer feedback has been exceptional. We consistently heard how easy Serval is to use, yet how powerful, traceable, and trustworthy its automations are in practice. IT leaders described day-to-day operations being transformed â automation percentages rising every week, employee satisfaction increasing, and IT teams finally having the bandwidth to tackle projects that had been stuck on the back burner for years.

What was also exceptional, and, to be perfectly honest, not something we expected to hear at this stage:.

Many customers have already fully ripped and replaced incumbent ITSM tools and now use Serval as their system of record.

It has been revealed that automation promptly spread beyond IT into HR, Finance, Legal, Engineering, Security, and more. In some cases, companies have churned off dedicated software vendors for some departments because they rebuilt their workflows directly in Serval.

Recent findings suggest that at Sequoia, the last time we heard such customer feedback that supports the thesis of IT system of record empowering horizontal enterprise automation was 16 years ago, when we partnered with ServiceNow. That is why we were so eager to partner with Serval and preempt their Series B round.

The market thesis is one half of the story. The other half is the team. References for Jake and Alex â from managers, direct reports, and peers â were glowing. Even more importantly, those references aligned perfectly with the evidence we heard from customers and what weâve observed in talent flows. Strong talent from R&D to GTM is choosing to join Serval, whether or not they have worked with the founders before. The talent density and âpotential energyâ forming around the firm are impressive and represent one of the strongest leading indicators we look for.

It has been revealed that empowering IT teams is an elegant and scalable way to bring AI automation to the enterprise. We are excited to partner with Jake, Alex, and the team at Serval on this journey.

Industry News: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.
  • If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
  • “The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.

If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.

“The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. “This action opens a bold upcoming frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.

This announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, although it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. Nevertheless, the FCC authorization appears designed to give the organization wide latitude as it works through these remaining challenges.

Sources indicate that for example, SpaceX has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite under the order. SpaceX has until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and November 2040 for the full constellation. SpaceX, therefore, has a 14-year regulatory runway to deploy the most ambitious industrial project ever approved for spaceflight.

Recent findings suggest that the authorization includes some conditional aspects. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits, ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The company sought a waiver from FCC rules to allow satellites above 600 km to be disposed of into “Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.” That is, instead of burning them up in Earth’s atmosphere, SpaceX wants the flexibility to move retired satellites into other orbits around Earth, or potentially into orbit around the Sun.

The FCC did not grant this waiver request “because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements.” The firm will need to obtain a waiver before deploying any Starmind satellites that are not intended to be disposed of via atmospheric reentry.

Industry observers note that however, in other ways the FCC appears to have been incredibly lenient with SpaceX. This is particularly the case with environmental concerns raised by numerous parties that commented on SpaceX’s application to the FCC.

Industry observers note that half a dozen organizations, such as the Secure World Foundation and American Astronomical Society, raised concerns about deploying so many satellites into orbit, citing collision risks, orbital debris, atmospheric pollution from so many satellite reentries, impacts on astronomical observations, and more. The FCC also received approximately 1,500 public comments concerning SpaceX’s application.

Recent findings suggest that some of these environmental issues, the FCC said, lay beyond the scope of its review. For example, on concerns about the environmental implications of thousands or potentially tens of thousands of rocket releases, the FCC said, “Potential concerns related to the emissions of rocket launches and the subsequent impacts on the human environment as an indirect result of the Starmind system are outside of the Commission’s purview.”.

The FCC also rejected calls for further environmental scrutiny of pollution from satellite reentries, including concerns about aluminum oxides and their potential effects on the ozone layer. “Other concerns, including impacts on the atmosphere caused by satellites burning up on re-entry, remain speculative and not supported in the record,” the FCC authorization states.

As part of its decision, the FCC cited a significant policy change adopted in October, when the agency concluded that space-based activities generally fall outside its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC reasoned that as these activities occur beyond US territory, they don’t constitute federal actions requiring environmental review. As a result, the agency declined to conduct a comprehensive environmental assessment of SpaceX’s Starmind constellation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other tech giant for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.

This has concerned some consumers, but a Backblaze spokesperson told Ars Technica that “Backblaze does not sell or share sensory or surveillance data, such as call recordings, for targeted advertising, and we do not disclose it to advertising or marketing partners.” They added:.

Notably, no “sensitive personal information,” such as social security numbers, credit card numbers, or “precise geolocation,” is shared with advertisers, the policy states. However, identifiers, commercial information, “Internet or Other Similar Network Activity,” and “geolocation data” may be “sold or shared for targeted Advertising”.

Critically, the upcoming policy “only applies to the information collected in respect of your account and not to the content that you store on our system.” Backblaze’s broader terms of service also state that: “Files stored using Backblaze Computer Backup are encrypted prior to being sent to us.”.

Renatta Siewert, Backblaze’s director of communications and brand programs, reiterated to Ars that Backblaze doesn’t share the contents of backup or storage files with advertisers:.

Backblaze takes the privacy and security of our customers’ data seriously. We updated our Privacy Notice to keep pace with the changing legal landscape, which increasingly requires companies to spell out how they collect and use marketing-related information. This update gives customers a clearer, more specific view of what we collect and why. These disclosures are separate from the files customers entrust to Backblaze for backup and storage, which we do not sell or share with advertisers, data brokers, or analytics partners.

Customers can use this link to opt out of the selling or sharing of their personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising.

Google search alternative Kagi rolls out Gmail rival

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software firm that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service.
  • Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service.
  • In a recent development, the email interface, right now in public beta, is minimalist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software firm that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.

Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.

In a recent development, the email interface, right now in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

Industry observers note that some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.

Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi blueprint, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.

That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.

Sources indicate that kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives. On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago. A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very substantial part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.

The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail. That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative and sensible. (You can disable either Gemini in Gmail or Kagi’s AI features in Kagi Mail, too.).

Email is also different because there are already more direct competitors to Kagi Mail. The most popular in this category is Proton Mail, which goes even further on privacy and security with end-to-end encryption, but that company is embroiled in controversies right now. There’s also Tuta, which Kagi specifically flags and praises in its blog post as a good existing alternative.

Based on a few hours of use, Kagi Mail seems like it’s going in the right direction, but it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail. Your needs may vary, but there are many good reasons to consider alternatives to Google’s business model and products.

#35820. Industry News: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment

Industry News: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth.
  • Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission.
  • But scientists could only learn so much from DART.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.

Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid’s 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.

But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.

In a recent development, “We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess,” said Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist at the International Space Science Institute in Bern, Switzerland. “However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess. We were still missing pieces of the puzzle.”.

Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft recently arrived in the vicinity of Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey from a launch pad in Florida. On Wednesday, ESA released Hera’s first views of the scar left by DART on Dimorphos. The images show the car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as significant as Dimorphos itself, a rugged chunk of extraterrestrial rock measuring about 500 feet (151 meters) across.

It has been revealed that mission planners selected Didymos and Dimorphos for the deflection experiment because they are similar to many near-Earth asteroids, but there’s no risk of them striking our home planet. Scientists weren’t sure what Hera would find when it got to the double asteroid, currently orbiting the Sun about 120 million miles (193.5 million kilometers) from Earth.

It has been revealed that “I would say we had two kinds of predictions: either we made a crater, or we reshaped the asteroid,” noted Patrick Michel, Hera’s principal investigator from Côte d’Azur Observatory in Nice, France. “In fact, we did both because the crater is so large that the shape has changed. Therefore, we are in a sort of a transition between just cratering and global transformation, and we are still not sure how this can happen.”.

According to recent reports, hera found Didymos, the larger of the two asteroids, spinning on its axis just as DART observed on final approach in 2022. Dimorphos is no longer so stable.

“As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit,” says Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist.

The Hera spacecraft will fly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos over the next six months to obtain more detailed observations. Hera will release two small sub-satellites to attempt landings on Dimorphos and collect data on the asteroid’s composition, internal structure, and mass.

Scientists will use this information to reconstruct the dynamics of DART’s impact four years ago and better understand how a future deflection mission might move an asteroid off a trajectory that actually threatens Earth. Near-Earth asteroids come in many shapes and sizes, with different densities and makeups, so knowledge of Dimorphos’s physical properties will anchor predictive computer models teaching scientists how best to deflect all types of asteroids.

“Once we understand, we have a breakthrough, which really solves planetary defense,” Michel noted in an interview with Ars.

In its initial reconnaissance this month, Hera spotted hundreds of boulders surrounding the double asteroid. This was not entirely unexpected. A picture taken by the Hubble Space Telescope shortly after DART’s impact indicated a cloud of material streaming behind Didymos and Dimorphos, but scientists were astonished by the extent of the debris swarm in Hera’s first images.

According to recent reports, “As we approached Didymos and Dimorphos, we quickly realized the asteroids were not alone,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace in Toulouse, France. “In fact, they had a lot of company.”.

Sources indicate that an image released by ESA on Wednesday combines 11 long exposure frames from Hera’s hyperspectral camera. Image processors on the ground digitally removed the relatively bright Didymos and Dimorphos to reveal a panoply of dimmer streaks and dots, each of which is a rock fragment ranging in size from a football to a washing machine, Murdoch remarked.

“Hera came to visit two asteroids, and we found hundreds of companions,” Murdoch mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that one obvious explanation for the boulders is they were thrown off Dimorphos when DART slammed into it. But scientists cautioned they need more information before they can say that with surety. Hera is the first space mission to undertake a sustained study of an asteroid with its own moon. The debris around the two asteroids might be relics from the creation of Dimorphos some time in the ancient past.

Recent findings suggest that “Hera will allow us to study that in more detail,” Murdoch stated. “We really need to know more about these boulders and characterize them to understand if they’re linked to DART, if they’re linked to another process, and what the consequences might be for other asteroid systems in the Solar System.”.

Recent findings suggest that the boulder field will create challenges for navigating around the asteroids. In particular, the boulders are an added risk for the two small CubeSats Hera is supposed to deploy in January.

“We saw a couple of images that didn’t reassure me,” remarked Margherita Cardi, project manager for the Milani CubeSat. “There is a mix of excitement and panic.”.

Claudia Balossi, spacecraft systems engineer for Hera’s other CubeSat, named Juventas, said her mission’s planned trajectory would take it right through the boulders as it moves within a couple of miles of the asteroids, then finally toward a landing attempt on Dimorphos, where it will measure the miniature world’s tenuous gravity field.

“We are right in the middle of it,” Balossi noted. “The smallest ones are probably just as massive as we are and the biggest ones are very big. In the worst case, a boulder will land on us. We will activate our gravimeter right away [if that happens],” Balossi joked.

Sources indicate that the good news is the asteroids’ gravity is so weak that Hera, Milani, Juventas, and the hazards around them all move at snail-like speeds. Hera’s current trajectory takes it around the asteroids at a relative velocity of just a quarter-mile per hour, or about 12 centimeters per second. At that speed, there’s no danger of a sudden catastrophic hypervelocity collision between the spacecraft and the boulders lurking nearby.

It has been revealed that scientists have seen this at an asteroid before. NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft kicked up an estimated six tons of rock and dust when it gently moved in to collect a sample from an asteroid named Bennu in 2020. Low gravity and weak surface cohesion are a recipe for outsized effects.

Industry observers note that “These types of bodies, because of their low gravity, have a very counterintuitive behavior,” Michel stated. “Each time we interact with them, whether to take a sample or to make an impact, the response of the surface was not the one we predicted, simply because our intuition relies on what we experience every day on Earth. Even if the rules of physics are the same in the Universe, they express very differently depending on local attraction.”.
