Years ago, some leading researchers told us that their objective was AGI. Eager to hear a coherent definition, we naively asked âhow do you define AGI?â. They paused, looked at each other tentatively, and then offered up whatâs since become something of a mantra in the field of AI: âwell, we each kind of have our own definitions, but weâll know it when we see it.â.

This vignette typifies our quest for a concrete definition of AGI. It has proven elusive.

While the definition is elusive, the reality is not. AGI is here, now.

Sources indicate that coding agents are the first example. There are more on the way.

Long-horizon agents are functionally AGI, and 2026 will be their year.

Before we go any further, itâs worth acknowledging that we do not have the moral authority to propose a technical definition of AGI.

In a recent development, we are investors. We study markets, founders, and the collision thereof: businesses.

According to recent reports, given that, ours is a functional definition, not a technical definition. New technical capabilities beg the Don Valentine question: so what?

The answer resides in real world impact.

Sources indicate that AGI is the ability to figure things out. Thatâs it.*.

It has been revealed that *We appreciate that such an imprecise definition will not settle any philosophical debates. Pragmatically speaking, what do you want if youâre trying to get something done? An AI that can just figure stuff out. How it happens is of less concern than the fact that it happens.

A human who can figure things out has some baseline knowledge, the ability to reason over that knowledge, and the ability to iterate their way to the answer.

An AI that can figure things out has some baseline knowledge (pre-training), the ability to reason over that knowledge (inference-time compute), and the ability to iterate its way to the answer (long-horizon agents).

According to recent reports, the first ingredient (knowledge / pre-training) is what fueled the original ChatGPT moment in 2022. The second (reasoning / inference-time compute) came with the release of o1 in late 2024. The third (iteration / long-horizon agents) came in the last few weeks with Claude Code and other coding agents crossing a capability threshold.

It has been revealed that generally intelligent people can work autonomously for hours at a time, making and fixing their mistakes and figuring out what to do next without being told. Generally intelligent agents can do the same thing. This is new.

Industry observers note that A founder messages his agent: âI need a developer relations lead. Someone technical enough to earn respect from senior engineers, but who actually enjoys being on Twitter. We sell to platform teams. Go.â.

Industry observers note that the agent starts with the obvious: LinkedIn searches for âDeveloper Advocateâ and âDevRelâ at competing companies â Datadog, Temporal, Langchain. It finds hundreds of profiles. But job titles donât reveal whoâs actually good at this.

It pivots to signal over credentials. It searches YouTube for conference talks. It finds 50+ speakers, then filters for those with talks that have strong engagement.

In a recent development, it cross-references those speakers with Twitter. Half have inactive accounts or just retweet their employerâs blog posts. Not what we want. But a dozen have real followings â they post real opinions, reply to people, and get engagement from developers. And their posts have real taste.

The agent narrows further. It checks whoâs been posting less frequently in the last three months. A drop in activity sometimes signals disengagement from their current role. Three names surface.

It researches those three. One just confirmed a fresh role â too late. One is a founder of a company that just raised funding â not leaving. The third is a senior DevRel at a Series D company that just did layoffs in marketing. Her last talk was about exactly the platform engineering space the startup targets. She has 14k Twitter followers and posts memes that actual engineers engage with. She hasnât updated her LinkedIn in two months.

It has been revealed that the agent drafts an email acknowledging her recent talk, the overlap with the startupâs ICP, and a specific note about the creative freedom a smaller team offers. It suggests a casual conversation, not a pitch.

Total time: 31 minutes. The founder has a shortlist of one instead of a JD posted to a job board.

Industry observers note that this is what it means to figure things out. Navigating ambiguity to accomplish a goal â forming hypotheses, testing them, hitting dead ends, and pivoting until something clicks. The agent didnât follow a script. It ran the same loop a great recruiter runs in their head, except it did it tirelessly in 31 minutes, without being told how.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear: agents still fail. They hallucinate, lose context, and sometimes charge confidently down exactly the wrong path. But the trajectory is unmistakable, and the failures are increasingly fixable.

Industry observers note that in last yearâs essay, we wrote about reasoning models as the most important new frontier for AI. Long-horizon agents push this paradigm further by allowing models to take actions and iterate over time.

Sources indicate that coaxing a model to think for longer is not trivial. A base reasoning model can think for seconds or minutes.

It has been revealed that two different technical approaches seem to both be working and scaling well: reinforcement learning and agent harnesses. The former approach teaches a model intrinsically to stay on track for longer by poking and prodding it to maintain focus during the training process. The latter designs specific scaffolding around the known limitations of models (memory hand-offs, compaction, and more).

Scaling reinforcement learning is the domain of the research labs. They have made exceptional progress on this front, from multi-agent systems to reliable tool use.

According to recent reports, designing great agent harnesses is the domain of the application layer. Some of the most beloved products on the market today are known for their exceptionally engineered agent harnesses: Manus, Claude Code, Factoryâs Droids, etc.

If thereâs one exponential curve to bet on, itâs the performance of long-horizon agents. METR has been meticulously tracking AIâs ability to complete long-horizon tasks. The rate of progress is exponential, doubling every ~7 months. If we trace out the exponential, agents should be able to work reliably to complete tasks that take human experts a full day by 2028, a full year by 2034, and a full century by 2037.

According to recent reports, soon youâll be able to hire an agent. Thatâs one litmus test for AGI (h/t: Sarah Guo).

It has been revealed that you can âhireâ GPT-5.2 or Claude or Grok or Gemini today. More examples are on the way:.

Medicine: OpenEvidenceâs Deep Consult functions as a specialist.

Law: Harveyâs agents function as an Associate.

Cybersecurity: XBOW functions as a pen-tester.

DevOps: Traversalâs agents function as an SRE.

GTM: Day AI functions as a BDR, SE, and Rev Ops leader.

Recruiting: Juicebox functions as a recruiter.

Math: Harmonicâs Aristotle functions as a mathematician.

Semiconductor Design: Ricursiveâs agents function as chip designers.

AI Researcher: GPT-5.2 and Claude function as AI researchers.

This has profound implications for founders.

The AI applications of 2023 and 2024 were talkers. Some were very sophisticated conversationalists! But their impact was limited.

According to recent reports, the AI applications of 2026 and 2027 will be doers. They will feel like colleagues. Usage will go from a few times a day to all-day, every day, with multiple instances running in parallel. Users wonât save a few hours here and there â theyâll go from working as an IC to managing a team of agents.

According to recent reports, remember all that talk of selling work? Now itâs possible.

What work can you accomplish? The capabilities of a long-horizon agent are drastically different than a single forward pass of a model. What new capabilities do long-horizon agents unlock in your domain? What tasks require persistence, where sustained attention is the bottleneck?

According to recent reports, how will you productize that work? How will your application interface evolve in your domain, as the UI of work grows from chatbot to agent delegation?

Recent findings suggest that can you do that work reliably? Are you obsessively improving your agent harness? Do you have a strong feedback loop?

How can you sell that work?Can you price and package to value and outcomes?

Itâs time to ride the long-horizon agent exponential.

Recent findings suggest that today, your agents can probably work reliably for ~30 minutes. But theyâll be able to perform a dayâs worth of work very soon â and a centuryâs worth of work eventually.

It has been revealed that what can you achieve when your intends are measured in centuries? A century is 200,000 clinical trials no oneâs cross-referenced. A century is every customer support ticket ever filed, finally mined for signal. A century is the entire U.S. tax code, refactored for coherence.

The ambitious version of your roadmap just became the realistic one.

In a recent development, amazon CloudWatch Omni alerts can now automatically create PagerDuty incidents, so notifications flow directly into your existing incident management workflows. This reduces mean time to resolution (MTTR) by eliminating manual notification steps and ensuring consistent incident workflows.

CloudWatch Omni is a fully managed AI-powered observability experience built on open standards that unifies monitoring for AI agents, applications, and infrastructure. PagerDuty is an incident management platform that routes alerts to the right on-call responders and coordinates their response. When an Omni alert fires, Omni creates a PagerDuty incident. In PagerDuty, Omni alerts follow your existing on-call schedules and escalation policies, so critical alerts reach the right responder wherever they are, at any hour. Omni alerts include severity, the affected service, and a link back to the related data in Omni, so responders have the context they need to diagnose the problem.

For PagerDuty integration in Amazon CloudWatch Omni regional availability, see Supported Regions for CloudWatch Omni.

AWS Lambda now supports orchestrating MicroVMs with Lambda durable functions

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (319 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, AWS reveals a developer preview of a new extension for orchestrating Lambda MicroVMs with Lambda durable functions.
  • It has been revealed that with Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient, multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries.
  • According to recent reports, the MicroVM extension is available as a developer preview for the AWS Durable Execution SDK for TypeScript and Python.

Today, AWS reveals a developer preview of a new extension for orchestrating Lambda MicroVMs with Lambda durable functions. The extension adds durable operations for running work on MicroVMs and managing their lifecycle. You can use the new operations to build software factories, security scanners, or orchestrate CI/CD jobs that run untrusted or agent-generated code in isolated sandboxes.

It has been revealed that with Lambda durable functions, you can build resilient, multi-step applications and AI workflows that run for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing and automatic retries. Lambda MicroVMs are a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for running user-generated or AI-generated code. With this launch, you can run individual tasks in a MicroVM or launch a MicroVM session, where tasks share the same files and memory. The durable function manages the MicroVM lifecycle and runs each task as a durable operation. It checkpoints progress, retries failed tasks, and refreshes MicroVM tokens as needed. A single durable function can orchestrate multiple MicroVMs in parallel, and you can trigger it from event sources such as Amazon SQS or Amazon EventBridge. An optional worker library runs inside your MicroVM image to receive tasks, send heartbeats, and report results.

According to recent reports, the MicroVM extension is available as a developer preview for the AWS Durable Execution SDK for TypeScript and Python. To get started, add the extensions package to your function alongside the Durable Execution SDK (JS/TS, Python) and add the MicroVM worker library (JS/TS, Python) to your MicroVM image. Developer preview features may change, so do not use them for production workloads. The extension is available in all AWS Regions that support Lambda durable functions and Lambda MicroVMs.

To learn more, see the MicroVM orchestration documentation and the sample application. To share feedback, open an issue in the Durable Execution SDK GitHub repository in JavaScript or Python.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that right now, there’s probably something you’re forgetting to do.
  • Also: I tried the Flowtica Verso AI notetaker expecting a gimmick – now it’s my newly introduced favorite MagSafe gadget.
  • Over the past few weeks, I tested two such devices that claim to refresh my failing memory, but with very different approaches.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that right now, there’s probably something you’re forgetting to do. Do you know what it is? Tech companies are wise to our absentmindedness, selling the solution back to us in the form of miced wearables that yearn to be our personal assistants.

Also: I tried the Flowtica Verso AI notetaker expecting a gimmick – now it’s my newly introduced favorite MagSafe gadget.

Over the past few weeks, I tested two such devices that claim to refresh my failing memory, but with very different approaches. One was Siri Recap, a beta feature on the latest Apple Watch that listens to your conversations and generates summaries. The other was the Pebble Index 01, a ring with a microphone and a button — and nothing else.

The two wearables illustrate how different companies are building the same product. The $75 Pebble Index 01 is open-source and easily integrated with plug-ins. Siri Recap is private and closed. The note-taking ring has one purpose. The Apple Watch has many. People control what the Index 01 notes. Apple Watch users are at the whims of Siri. But which actually does the job better? I tested the Index 01 to see for myself.

Industry observers note that pebble’s Index 01 is not exactly a smart ring like the Oura Ring — it can’t track your heart rate or tell you how well you slept. Instead, it’s essentially a specialized mic with its own app, or a personalized agent, if that agent were wrapped around your finger. The ring comes in three colors: silver, gold, or black, and fits sizes six through 13. You can use it with or without an internet connection, and the Index 01 stores up to 5 minutes of recordings without your phone present.

Also: I watched a movie on Meta’s new VR glasses – it was awesome, but isolating.

According to recent reports, wearing the device felt like I was wearing another smart ring. While I didn’t sleep with it on, I definitely could have — and wouldn’t have noticed its presence. It was discreet and comfortable. It’s water-resistant, so I wore the ring while washing my hands and doing the dishes with no problems. It’s not rechargeable, with a battery life of around two to three years, depending on usage. Once it dies, you’ll have no choice but to buy another. Thankfully, $75 per ring isn’t a bad price.

Sources indicate that the Pebble Index 01 is a straightforward wearable. Have a stroke of genius or a grocery item you don’t want to forget? Press the button on the ring’s crown, and speak into the microphone. Your note will appear in the accompanying Pebble app, where it’s organized into shopping lists, to-dos, or customized lists.

I got a notification each time a note was recorded on the app, so I could quality-check my notes before they’re sorted, or redo any errors. The microphone didn’t pick up what was said or misheard my note a few times, but these are easily editable within the app. Most of the time, the Index 01 works perfectly fine.

The ring is designed to connect to various plugins, such as Claude Code, Muse, or Notion, so ring wearers can control where their queries go and use the device as a wearable agent. Because it’s so easy to connect to other apps, you can use the ring as if it’s an extension of your phone, asking the ring to turn on the smart lights through one app or vibe code a website in another. I connected my Index 01 to Claude, and sent it questions while my phone was out of reach.

Sources indicate that I’ve found the ring to be most useful for the random stuff in my life. As I juggle work tasks, friends’ birthdays, holiday looks, and my own growing list of to-dos, the Index 01 helped me to organize those fleeting moments where an important memory popped up I was too distracted to remember.

Industry observers note that the ring has helped me note important dates. It reminded me to ask my boyfriend about a DJ event I wanted to go to (I had even forgotten that I made that note in the first place). I’ve talked through my Saturday to-do list with the ring, organizing the list purely by voice. In fact, lists have become one of the main ways I’ve used the ring. The last list I added to consists of Christmas decorations and holiday outing ideas.

One gripe is that you have to manually create upcoming lists on the app. You can’t just make a new one verbally. I organize my to-do lists by date and keep separate lists for products I’ve been meaning to buy, as well as for notes to self and writing goals. These ideas are often stray thoughts I have one moment and forget the next, but the ring can capture and contain a single idea, holding me more accountable for my own creativity.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future.

Don’t get me wrong: I’m a pen-and-paper writer through and through, and won’t be ditching my physical agenda when it comes to organizing and time-stamping my to-do list. Nevertheless, the Index 01 assisted me when I didn’t have my notepad handy — or when I thought of something I’d need to remember in the distant future.

It has been revealed that the bottom line? The ring has certainly helped me to remember more. Pebble accomplishes this, in part, by designing the technology to swiftly organize and sort spoken notes. It also helps me to remember by simply forcing me to speak notes out loud — not just think them.

After testing the Index 01, I’m less convinced that ambient-listening devices are the solution to the forgetfulness crisis. The Pebble Index 01 helped me remember better because I could speak to it directly, forcing me to take an active role in choosing what to note and prioritize. With the always-listening Siri Recap, I had far less control over what Siri deemed noteworthy enough to summarize.

Sources indicate that testing Siri Recap resulted in a lot of useless conversation summaries, listening for any voices at all without discernment. At one point, it even picked up on my TikTok scrolling and made a note on it. Another time, it summarized “Clubkid,” a movie I had watched with my friend, creating a note about drug addiction and child custody, as if I were the one experiencing these things and not the main character of the movie.

According to recent reports, it was always listening. In doing so, it summarized information in the app that I had no use for, or made me sift through small talk to find a conversation tidbit I was looking for.

Also: I tested Siri Recap on my Apple Watch for a week – then turned it off, for good.

In a recent development, tech companies are pushing all-seeing and all-listening devices at consumers left and right, but my time with the Index 01 proved to me that the best technology is rarely invasive. It can be as simple as a ring with a microphone and a helpful, accompanying app.

I’d recommend the Pebble Index 01 to anyone interested in a upcoming approach to note-taking or memory jogging. This device is not only straightforward to use and easy to customize with plug-ins, but it’s also cheaper than its competitors, at $75. It helped me keep track of stray thoughts, dates, and my long list of personal and work-related to-dos.

I can genuinely say it helped me remember things I would’ve forgotten, and I appreciate its minimal approach more than Apple’s always-on listening, which both comes with its own privacy concerns and is less efficient.

Industry observers note that sometimes you meet a founder who is so good that you want to back them no matter what they are working on. Just as rarely, you meet a firm whose vision is so singular, it feels both inevitable and differentiated at the same time. When I first sat down with Ben and Asher Spector to discuss Flapping Airplanes, I felt both of these to be true at once.

Ben is a founder of Prod, which has quickly become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley. Asher, one year Benâs senior, is a former debate champion turned Stanford statistics Ph.D. The brothers have an eye for raw talent, and aged 25 and 26 respectively, they are building the âyoung personâs AGI lab.â Their co-founder Aidan Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at Neuralink for three years while in college at Georgia Tech. Ben and Asher believe that raw talent â the type of people who would previously have gone on to do Ph.D.s or join quant firms â are the key to unlocking the next phase of AI development. This stands in sharp contrast to the approach of focusing on âbrand nameâ AI talent at any price, which seems so in vogue right now.

There is something else that is countercultural about this lab too: they recognize that scale alone is not enough. Indeed, the lab is predicated on this notion. There is only one Internet, and weâve run out of it. Data is the bottleneck today to further AI scaling, not compute. Todayâs AI models are wildly inefficient, something that Dwarkesh Patel has recently hammered home in his interviews with Andrej Karpathy, Richard Sutton and others. Flapping Airplanes is dedicated to searching for a more data-efficient AI. The companyâs name is a nod to a more biological notion of machine intelligence.

One of the fundamental debates right now in AI is around scaling vs. research. The scaling paradigm argues for dedicating a huge amount of societyâs resources, as much as the economy can muster, toward scaling up todayâs LLMs, in the hopes that this will lead to AGI. The research paradigm argues that we are 2-3 research breakthroughs away from an âAGIâ intelligence, and as a result, we should dedicate resources to long-running research, especially projects that may take 5-10 years to come to fruition.

While the divide between these two schools of thought is far from absolute â research breakthroughs make compute investments more efficient, and GPUs are required for net newly introduced research â they each lead to different tradeoffs. A compute-first approach would prioritize cluster scale above all else, and would heavily favor short-term wins (on the order of 1-2 years) over long-term bets (on the order of 5-10 years). A research-first approach would spread bets temporally, and should be willing to make lots of bets that have a low absolute probability of working, but that collectively expand the search space for what is possible.

In a recent development, one concern I have had is that by starving Ph.D. programs of talent, and by reallocating a lot of this talent to scale-oriented work (as opposed to fundamental research), we could actually push out the AGI timeline. As I noted in a previous blog post, âcorporate politics tends to favor in vogue, consensus ideas over more radical, unpopular ones â the very kinds of ideas that can take years to prove worthwhile, and which scientific breakthroughs often depend on.â Flapping Airplanes is explicitly intended to provide a Ph.D.-like experience â true research independence, long-time horizons â while bridging the pay gap between academia and Substantial Tech.

One of the biggest learnings of the last decade in AI is the dramatic economic value of fundamental scientific progress. Since academia seems ill-suited to compete with Substantial Tech on this dimension right now, especially in AI, Flapping Airplanes is taking this into their own hands. And they are focused on precisely the problem that is likely to define the next wave of AI: building models inspired by the data efficiency of biology. With that as a north star, the organization will make bets in a variety of directions to get there.

There are two coherent motives right now in AI. One is the profit motive, and this should inspire all application builders, given the tremendous opportunity ahead. As I have noted on many occasions, AI is so underpenetrated relative to the capability set available, it is likely to create a golden age for builders for many years to come. There is a large profit pool available, and we are in the very earliest stages of generating it.

In a recent development, the second coherent motive in AI is AGI, predicated on the belief that now that weâve unlocked a machine intelligence, we should push toward upleveling that intelligence. Economically, progress in this direction is likely to be extremely valuable. The question is how to take on this objective in an efficient way, with a reasonable probability that resources invested will translate into long-term positive results. Flapping Airplanes is a pure play in that direction.

One of the most attractive aspects for me in partnering with Flapping Airplanes was the team. I have met nearly every candidate that has interviewed at Flapping Airplanes, and certainly every person the manufacturer has hired. This is one of the best teams Iâve ever seen assembled at the beginning of such an ambitious journey.

There are two core beliefs that make Flapping Airplanes different for top talent:.

A belief that young people have always unlocked fundamental science in the past (Einstein was 26 during his âMiracle Yearâ).

A conviction that AI research is not a mystical domain for experts, but a domain learnable by anyone that is smart and ambitious.

With just these two premises, Flapping Airplanes is at odds with a prestige-obsessed culture in the Valley right now. It is exactly this obsession with substance and with raw individual talent that made Ben so successful at Prod, and it is this âflame spottingâ ability that gives me confidence in the courageous effort that is now Flapping Airplanes.

If you are interested to join, please reach out to recruiting@flappingairplanes.com.

Latest Update: Not Just Nvidia: Inside Team Trump’s Takeover of Intel

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your manufacturer.
  • In a recent development, do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit.
  • Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your manufacturer. Right now. Or else.

In a recent development, do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”.

Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”.

Recent findings suggest that days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”.

President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the firm’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official claims. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”.

Sources indicate that documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

Recent findings suggest that “It's just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what's best for the company in the short or long term, what's best for shareholders, but what's best for politics and what the government is demanding.”.

“That's not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you're talking about the world's most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that's a huge problem.”.

Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

The parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the firm’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office.

During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.

In a recent development, at the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, indicates the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times.) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “a horrible, horrible thing.” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration mentioned it was renegotiating the deals.

In a recent development, the same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s fresh CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing's military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.

Sources indicate that two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted, "The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem.".

It has been revealed that tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change, Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.

It has been revealed that “The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”.

Neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the tech giant. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told the Wall Street Journal. “I mentioned, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”.

Sources indicate that “I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.

According to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the Fresh York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the company’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.

In a recent development, then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he noted, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”.

Intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the manufacturer,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.

But they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the organization. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”.

Sources indicate that on August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and said. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”.

Sources indicate that inside the organization, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”.

Not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted. “Who would not want to make deals like that?”.

Deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump revealed that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang. The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I noted, if I'm going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.

In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”.

In court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the company “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”.

In a recent development, the attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said on the company’s quarterly earnings call that it did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The Newly introduced York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.

“Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this organization, not even a little bit,” Huang said during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported. “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.
  • Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.
  • In the Prod community, they talk about founders as âtime travelersâ rather than visionaries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

In the Prod community, they talk about founders as âtime travelersâ rather than visionaries. Founders donât see the future, they teleport there.

I think this is true in more ways than first meets the eye. To extend the analogy of a chess game (which I recently used in an essay on the AI race and which Will Manidis also articulated beautifully in his essay on âEndgame Playâ), outside observers see startups as temporally sequential, with a beginning (inception/ seed stage), middle (product-market fit/ growth stage), and end (IPO/ scale-up). However, the best founders actually live in all three of these phases simultaneously.

In a recent development, opening: The opening phase of a startup involves the âmagicâ of transforming from a few people with an idea into a âstartup.â Silicon Valley excels at this magic, and Paul Graham is the prophet of the opening. There are many opening strategies, but the lean startup model has proven itself to be the most repeatable one. The ecosystem around company formation is important because foundational decisions made at this stage are difficult to change later, and so wisdom pays dividends.

Midgame: The midgame of a startup begins once product-market fit has been reached. Many startups fail before ever reaching this stage. Product-market fit requires deeply understanding a customerâs need, and building a solution. Once product-market fit has been reached, you need to build a tech giant â figure out how to hire people, manage people, and improve the product. You need to achieve some type of takeoff, forward momentum that will allow the business to grow from something tiny and irrelevant into something meaningful and notable. Board members exist to transmit inter-generational knowledge on midgame play. Since the nature of the midgame is always evolving, founders need to filter this through their own prism to arrive at truth.

Endgame: The endgame of a startup is the infinite future â itâs never really reached. The endgame is vital, because without a vision of the future, the present has very little value â see the recent SaaSpocalypse. Elon Musk is the prophet of the endgame, he has always focused on the hardest problems, knowing that ambitious problems attract excellent people and unleash them to do their best work.

In a recent development, some startups seem uniquely engineered for the opening, some for the midgame, and some for the endgame. A hot AI company from Stanford students is engineered for the opening game â they will easily be able to recruit friends and a bike ride to Sand Hill road easily yields capital. A vertical SaaS company is engineered for the midgame â getting off the ground is hard and recruiting the early team is challenging, but once you unlock PMF, thereâs a clear path for how to scale it up. And a deep tech company is engineered for the endgame, itâs always clear from the moment of inception why that company should pass the âwho cares?â test.

According to recent reports, every startup has a different set of challenges depending on what parts of the game are structurally easier and harder. For example, a startup with a weak endgame story will struggle to raise funding without immense traction. A startup with a strong opening story is at risk of hubris, employees thinking the tech giant has reached the promised land, when nothing substantial has been achieved. And the âvalley of deathâ is famous in deep tech, precisely because a strong endgame story is always preceded by a long, fatigued midgame. The #1 piece of advice I give friends who are starting companies is to be aware of these biases, and explicitly combat them.

What is so incredible about the best companies, and the best founders, is that they appear to be playing the opening, midgame and endgame simultaneously. In the best companies, it is always early days and there is a big dream ahead (the opening vibe), even many years in. This is how Clay feels, even though the company is almost ten years old. Similarly, the best startups often have midgame characteristics at the opening â within a few months, they can show traction and improvement, creating a sense of forward momentum. For example, RunwayMLâs incredible open-source growth, years before Stable Diffusion. And finally, the best companies create a feeling of inevitability early, such that employees genuinely feel like they are moving the world forward. For example, Anduril pioneering modern defense tech.

One phrase Iâve often used to describe the best founders is, âNo matter what happens, they are going to win.â Alex Wangâs incredible journey at Scale from strength to strength was an early and illustrative example of this concept for me. The journey of Crusoe from crypto miner to AI factory builder is another great story of grit and judgement. What has crystalized for me now is seeing a superstructure that makes this possible â these founders are constantly holding the opening, midgame and endgame in their minds at the same time, and hence they are able to create a flexible, nimble culture that is always reinventing itself, and they are much quicker in adjusting their business strategy when the times are changing.

Recent findings suggest that my advice to founders is therefore this: No matter where you are in your journey, donât think about your business sequentially. Force yourself to play all three games at once â when planning product decisions, when making hires, when pitching investors. If you are in the midgame, you still need to care about opening style hires that could change the business. If you are in the opening, you need to think about the endgame, because thatâs what will inspire others to join you and help turn your vision into reality. And if you are in the endgame, you should still care about midgame momentum and opening creativity â thatâs how you will become absolutely massive. As you build your company, each of these narratives should be getting stronger â you canât just focus on the one that seems immediately in front of you.

Hair loss isn’t always dramatic. It can be incremental. You start noticing a bit more scalp in harsh bathroom lighting, a tiny bald spot when you tie your hair up in a ponytail. The shower drain is more clogged than usual. Not long ago, hair-loss treatments meant topical remedies, supplements, or a flight to Turkey. Luckily, red-light therapy brings the potential for hair regrowth into your home—no clinical appointment required.

In a recent development, beyond skin rejuvenation, clinical studies suggest red-light therapy can help energize hair follicles, increase blood circulation in the scalp, reduce inflammation, and lower dihydrotestosterone levels—a hormone that causes hair loss and thinning. Red-light therapy also supports adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, which helps provide oxygen and blood flow to the scalp and triggers follicles to remain in the hair growth phase.

According to recent reports, to determine the best red-light therapy for hair growth, I tapped five WIRED tech reviewers who've dealt with hair loss themselves. We assessed red-light caps, hands-free helmets with full scalp coverage, and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) or photobiomodulation devices for 16 weeks. Along the way, I reviewed the research, spoke with dermatologists, and tracked ease of use. These are the favorites that produced meaningful results and earned our trust.

To start, I consulted board-certified dermatologists and referred to clinical trials to help determine what features to look for when shopping for a device. I test these devices with several tech reviewers on our team, all of whom have personal experience with hair thinning or loss to different degrees. Most of these at-home gadgets call for a 16-week treatment cycle. We follow the brands' directions and record any visible results along the way.

It has been revealed that we monitor changes in hair count, hair density, and scalp health, but effectiveness is only one of the factors we consider. We also judge ease of use, functionality, and comfort. We note the specific wavelengths of light and whether the treatment options feel tolerable or difficult to integrate into everyday routines.

We also prioritize safety, checking for FDA clearance, automatic shut-off features, and overall durability of the design. To date, our testers have not experienced any side effects, but we would have documented them had they.

I'm testing the Foreo Flip Play and the Theradome PRO Laser Hair Growth Helmet LH80.

My hairstylist mentioned that my hair felt thicker, and I noticed less breakage and hair caught in bristles when brushing. My balding roommate also tested the CurrentBody helmet, and he noted that his hair also felt thicker and that there was new growth around the scalp.

She didn’t find any reaction on my scalp, either, from four months of using the device, and my roots look thicker all around my head.

Feels a little pointless to look outdoor-ready when you can’t actually use it on the go. It also got too hot for me to wear comfortably. —Nena Farrell.

Does Red-Light Therapy Work for Hair Loss?

In a recent development, yes—research suggests low-level light therapy can work for certain types of hair loss, such as androgenetic alopecia, also known as male or female pattern hair loss. It can help increase hair count, thickness, and density by stimulating hair follicles and boosting cellular activity in the scalp.

That mentioned, results depend heavily on the type and severity of hair loss. Red-light therapy works best in cases of mild to moderate thinning and may be less effective for advanced hair loss or scarring conditions like cicatricial alopecia. Consistency also matters. You typically need regular, ongoing use to maintain results, and benefits can diminish if treatments stop.

What Wavelength of Red Light Is Best for Hair Restoration?

According to the American Hair Loss Association, wavelengths in the range of 630 to 680 nanometers are ideal for hair regrowth. These wavelengths are known to support increased blood flow to the scalp, boost cellular activity, and help reduce inflammation. Some clinical studies specifically cite 650 nanometers as an especially effective wavelength.

Industry observers note that red-light devices that use medical-grade laser diodes tend to deliver more targeted and consistent light than standard LEDs, but both can stimulate hair follicles at the right wavelengths. For best results, look for FDA-cleared devices that list their wavelengths and power output.

How to Use Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth.

Sources indicate that consistency is the most important part of any red-light therapy routine. Most devices require at least three months of use before noticeable results are observed, and some may take longer. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as treatment schedules vary by device, but most recommend sessions three to five times per week. The hair growth is preserved only with continued use, so you’ll need ongoing maintenance sessions.

Always start with a clean and dry scalp so the light can reach your hair follicles without interference from oils or styling products. Some devices include protective eyewear, and if yours does, wear it during treatment. Make sure to wipe the device down with a gentle disinfectant before or after each session to prevent buildup on the LEDs.

Topical regrowth treatments can complement red-light therapy and may help support thicker hair. A few randomized clinical trials suggest that combining minoxidil (2 percent or 5 percent) with red-light therapy can improve hair density and encourage faster regrowth compared to using either treatment alone. For a natural alternative, some research has found rosemary oil to produce results comparable to 2 percent minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia, though the evidence isn’t as extensive as it is for minoxidil.

If you’re pregnant or have an underlying medical condition, talk to your healthcare provider before starting any form of red-light therapy.

Is Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth Safe?

According to recent reports, yes—for most people, red-light therapy is considered a safe and noninvasive treatment with minimal side effects when used as intended. Still, it's always worth consulting a health care professional before starting any sort of treatment. This is especially the case for anyone with photosensitive conditions or autoimmune disorders that affect light sensitivity.

I prefer devices that are FDA-cleared because it means they've met certain safety standards for consumer use. But keep in mind that the clearance process is less rigorous than the FDA approval pathway, as it just requires manufacturers to prove their product is “substantially equivalent” to an already legally marketed device. Also, FDA clearance isn't a guarantee of results; it simply means it's considered safe to use as directed at home.

With code shipping at a breakneck pace, how does observability keep up? Rustam and Achille built agents to watch the agents.

With code shipping at a breakneck pace, how does observability keep up? Rustam and Achille built agents to watch the agents.

Industry observers note that AI was supposed to make our lives easier. Yes, it can write our code for us. AI generates about half of Googleâs code, while companies like Anthropic rely on agents close to 100 percent of the time. But as that code stacks up, itâs harder and harder to tell when your product is doing the right or wrong things for your customers.

Firetiger is here to help. Firetiger is a newly introduced kind of observability product. Rather than expecting engineering to manage traditional events, dashboards and incidents, Firetiger handles all of that for you. Their agents are running 24/7, looking out for your customers, major and small. The Firetiger agent finds anomalies, checks if theyâre real and who theyâre impacting, and fixes them before your customers even notice if something went wrong.

Firetigerâs agents are keeping uptime numbers high and customers happy everywhere, from the biggest companies in the world to the fastest-growing startups in Silicon Valley. The product is available fully self-service for anyone to use.

Rustam and Achille have felt the pain theyâre solving firsthand. As VP of Product at Cloudflare, Rustam led teams that shipped infrastructure to billions of customers, while Achille built observability and solved scaling problems at Twitch, Segment and Twilio. They knew there had to be a better wayâand with Firetiger, theyâve built exactly that.

Congrats on the launch! Weâre thrilled to be your partners.

#35795. Tech Report: The 6 Best Latte Machines for Automatic Espresso Drinks (2026)
